Title: Inside Maryland High School Football: A Wild Finish in Cumberland and More Forfeits
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6
Rise and Reclaim is alive and well in Cumberland, Maryland, as the Fort Hillfootballteam continued its redemption tour with a heart-stopping 43-42 victory over Bridgeport (W.Va.) on Friday.

## **Four Touchdowns in Less Than 8 Minutes**
The game featured four touchdowns in the final 7:36, a successful two-point conversion in the closing minute, and a missed field goal on the final play in one of the most dramatic finishes this season.
The victory marked the second straight week Fort Hill avenged a 2025 loss as it continues its quest to reclaim its position as the state’s top 1A program. Fort Hill won four straight state championships before falling in last year’s state final, prompting the “Rise and Reclaim” motto for 2026. Fort Hill took a big step in that direction last week with a 35-21 victory over Hollidaysburg (Pa.). But Bridgeport was a different kind of monster.
Last year, Bridgeport handed Fort Hill a 49-14 thrashing in West Virginia, Fort Hill’s most lopsided regular-season loss since 2012. Friday’s rematch at Greenway Avenue Stadium carried historical significance, marking Bridgeport’s first game outside West Virginia after 1,098 consecutive in-state contests dating to 1921. The Sentinels again found themselves in trouble Friday, falling behind 21-7 before Bridgeport scored on a 70-yard play in the closing seconds of the second quarter to take a 28-14 halftime lead.
Fort Hill rallied to tie the game at 28 in the third quarter, setting up a wild finish.
Bridgeport took a 35-28 lead with 7:36 remaining, but Brady O’Neal answered 62 seconds later with a 78-yard touchdown pass to Carson Bender. Bridgeport again surged ahead, 42-35, before a three-minute Fort Hill drive was capped by Neek Taylor’s 7-yard scoring run, making it 42-41. There was no hesitation about going for two.
“When we started the next drive [down 42-35], everyone knew we’d be going for two,” Fort Hill coach Zach Alkire said.
After Bridgeport burned a timeout, Fort Hill called a quick pitch to the left. The wing got just enough of a block to give Taylor the room he needed to barely cross the goal line, putting Fort Hill ahead 43-42 with 51 seconds remaining.

## **Four Touchdowns in Less Than 8 Minutes**
Bridgeport quickly moved into field-goal range, aided by a defensive pass-interference penalty. An encroachment penalty moved the final attempt from 44 to 39 yards, but the kick had the distance and sailed just wide right, sending Fort Hill to 5-0.
“The sideline went nuts,” Alkire said. “Kids running off the field, hugging. There was a lot of excitement, and we needed that.”

## **100 Wins, 46 Years in the Making**
Washington defeated Nandua (Va.), 20-10, in a contest that could easily be overlooked among the more than 100 games played by Maryland high schools this past weekend.
For Washington, however, it was anything but ordinary. The victory marked the program’s 100th varsity win — a milestone 46 years in the making.
Washington launched its first varsity football team in 1980 and lost its debut 42-0 to James M. Bennett. That proved to be a sign of things to come.
Except for the COVID-19 pandemic season in 2020, Washington has put a varsity team on the field every year since 1980. During that time, Washington has had only two winning seasons: 7-4 in 1989 and 8-5 in 2003. Yet the program has persevered despite finishing at or near the bottom of the Bayside standings for much of its history.
Perhaps the times are changing for this tiny school, which has about 600 students in grades 8-12.
Alec Meintzer inherited the program in 2023 while it was mired in an 18-game losing streak. That streak eventually reached 38 games before Washington broke through with a 16-6 victory over North East-Cecil last season. The win sparked something bigger: Washington finished 5-5, its first non-losing season since 2003.
Meintzer stepped down after the season, and Tremont White has taken over. This year’s team is officially 2-2, as the MPSSAA ruled that a scheduled season opener at Northampton (Va.) was a no-contest since the game was not played.
Now Washington has a chance to reach 3-2 for the first time since 1998 when it faces Arcadia (Va.) on Friday. The Jaguars defeated Arcadia, 36-16, last season.

## **Forfeits, No-Contests Becoming an Unwanted Trend**
The Maryland high school football season has reached the halfway point, and an unusual number of games have disappeared from the schedule because of forfeits, no-contests, or teams dropping games altogether.
The latest came this past weekend in Prince George’s County. According to one of the head coaches, an altercation in the handshake line after the Oxon Hill-Potomac game in Week 4 resulted in both teams forfeiting their Week 5 contests. The two teams will also play their remaining games this season on Saturdays.
According to one of the head coaches, an altercation in the handshake line following the Oxon Hill-Potomac game in Week 4 resulted in both teams forfeiting their Week 5 contests.
It is the latest in a growing list of unusual circumstances that have taken games off the schedule this season.
North Point and Westlake forfeited their season openers in Charles County because of what was termed out-of-season contact violations. Maryland School for the Deaf received a forfeit victory when its scheduled opponent disbanded the week of the game. Annapolis Area Christian has forfeited two games because of a lack of healthy players.
Weather has also played a role. Northampton (Va.) canceled its scheduled game at Washington because of what was described as “extreme heat,” while weather-related no-contests cost Flowers and Wise games from their schedules.
The situation has been particularly interesting at Edmondson-Westside. Through five weeks, the team has played only two games. One scheduled game was a forfeit, and two others were never played after Hancock and Benjamin Franklin dropped their football programs before the season.
This past weekend, Sidwell Friends, which rejoined the Mid-Atlantic Conference this season, forfeited its league opener at St. James on Saturday, citing not enough healthy players.
Meanwhile, Central Maryland Christian, down to 18 players, has reduced its regular-season schedule to four games.
While the reasons are varied, the result is the same: fewer opportunities for players to compete and an increasingly unpredictable high school football schedule.

## **Crofton Remains Unbeaten**
Crofton was featured early this season after what was then considered an upset victory over Old Mill.
Now, the Wildcats have established themselves as the team to beat in Anne Arundel County. Crofton is the county’s lone 5-0 team and one of just 21 undefeated teams remaining in the MPSSAA.
Dominic Jackson delivered the latest heroics, scoring on a 3-yard run to lift Crofton to a 20-17 overtime victory over Chesapeake-AA.
The teams tied at 14 after regulation. Gary Windsor gave Chesapeake-AA a 17-14 lead in the first overtime with a 27-yard field goal, but Crofton answered with a touchdown to complete the comeback and remain unbeaten.

## **Got Your Number**
Northwestern-PG edged Bladensburg, 22-20, over the weekend, marking the third consecutive year the Wildcats have beaten the Mustangs.
While the streak is notable, it is even more remarkable that Bladensburg is the only team Northwestern-PG has beaten since 2019.
Since midseason 2019, Northwestern-PG is 4-2 against Bladensburg but 0-53 against all other opponents. The Wildcats’ last victory over anyone other than Bladensburg came on Oct. 12, 2019, when Northwestern-PG thrashed DuVal, 47-6.

texts.0: Rise and Reclaim is alive and well in Cumberland, Maryland, as the Fort Hillfootballteam continued its redemption tour with a heart-stopping 43-42 victory over Bridgeport (W.Va.) on Friday.
texts.1:
## **Four Touchdowns in Less Than 8 Minutes**
The game featured four touchdowns in the final 7:36, a successful two-point conversion in the closing minute, and a missed field goal on the final play in one of the most dramatic finishes this season.
The victory marked the second straight week Fort Hill avenged a 2025 loss as it continues its quest to reclaim its position as the state’s top 1A program. Fort Hill won four straight state championships before falling in last year’s state final, prompting the “Rise and Reclaim” motto for 2026. Fort Hill took a big step in that direction last week with a 35-21 victory over Hollidaysburg (Pa.). But Bridgeport was a different kind of monster.
Last year, Bridgeport handed Fort Hill a 49-14 thrashing in West Virginia, Fort Hill’s most lopsided regular-season loss since 2012. Friday’s rematch at Greenway Avenue Stadium carried historical significance, marking Bridgeport’s first game outside West Virginia after 1,098 consecutive in-state contests dating to 1921. The Sentinels again found themselves in trouble Friday, falling behind 21-7 before Bridgeport scored on a 70-yard play in the closing seconds of the second quarter to take a 28-14 halftime lead.
Fort Hill rallied to tie the game at 28 in the third quarter, setting up a wild finish.
Bridgeport took a 35-28 lead with 7:36 remaining, but Brady O’Neal answered 62 seconds later with a 78-yard touchdown pass to Carson Bender. Bridgeport again surged ahead, 42-35, before a three-minute Fort Hill drive was capped by Neek Taylor’s 7-yard scoring run, making it 42-41. There was no hesitation about going for two.
“When we started the next drive [down 42-35], everyone knew we’d be going for two,” Fort Hill coach Zach Alkire said.
After Bridgeport burned a timeout, Fort Hill called a quick pitch to the left. The wing got just enough of a block to give Taylor the room he needed to barely cross the goal line, putting Fort Hill ahead 43-42 with 51 seconds remaining.
texts.2:
## **Four Touchdowns in Less Than 8 Minutes**
Bridgeport quickly moved into field-goal range, aided by a defensive pass-interference penalty. An encroachment penalty moved the final attempt from 44 to 39 yards, but the kick had the distance and sailed just wide right, sending Fort Hill to 5-0.
“The sideline went nuts,” Alkire said. “Kids running off the field, hugging. There was a lot of excitement, and we needed that.”
texts.3:
## **100 Wins, 46 Years in the Making**
Washington defeated Nandua (Va.), 20-10, in a contest that could easily be overlooked among the more than 100 games played by Maryland high schools this past weekend.
For Washington, however, it was anything but ordinary. The victory marked the program’s 100th varsity win — a milestone 46 years in the making.
Washington launched its first varsity football team in 1980 and lost its debut 42-0 to James M. Bennett. That proved to be a sign of things to come.
Except for the COVID-19 pandemic season in 2020, Washington has put a varsity team on the field every year since 1980. During that time, Washington has had only two winning seasons: 7-4 in 1989 and 8-5 in 2003. Yet the program has persevered despite finishing at or near the bottom of the Bayside standings for much of its history.
Perhaps the times are changing for this tiny school, which has about 600 students in grades 8-12.
Alec Meintzer inherited the program in 2023 while it was mired in an 18-game losing streak. That streak eventually reached 38 games before Washington broke through with a 16-6 victory over North East-Cecil last season. The win sparked something bigger: Washington finished 5-5, its first non-losing season since 2003.
Meintzer stepped down after the season, and Tremont White has taken over. This year’s team is officially 2-2, as the MPSSAA ruled that a scheduled season opener at Northampton (Va.) was a no-contest since the game was not played.
Now Washington has a chance to reach 3-2 for the first time since 1998 when it faces Arcadia (Va.) on Friday. The Jaguars defeated Arcadia, 36-16, last season.
texts.4:
## **Forfeits, No-Contests Becoming an Unwanted Trend**
The Maryland high school football season has reached the halfway point, and an unusual number of games have disappeared from the schedule because of forfeits, no-contests, or teams dropping games altogether.
The latest came this past weekend in Prince George’s County. According to one of the head coaches, an altercation in the handshake line after the Oxon Hill-Potomac game in Week 4 resulted in both teams forfeiting their Week 5 contests. The two teams will also play their remaining games this season on Saturdays.
According to one of the head coaches, an altercation in the handshake line following the Oxon Hill-Potomac game in Week 4 resulted in both teams forfeiting their Week 5 contests.
It is the latest in a growing list of unusual circumstances that have taken games off the schedule this season.
North Point and Westlake forfeited their season openers in Charles County because of what was termed out-of-season contact violations. Maryland School for the Deaf received a forfeit victory when its scheduled opponent disbanded the week of the game. Annapolis Area Christian has forfeited two games because of a lack of healthy players.
Weather has also played a role. Northampton (Va.) canceled its scheduled game at Washington because of what was described as “extreme heat,” while weather-related no-contests cost Flowers and Wise games from their schedules.
The situation has been particularly interesting at Edmondson-Westside. Through five weeks, the team has played only two games. One scheduled game was a forfeit, and two others were never played after Hancock and Benjamin Franklin dropped their football programs before the season.
This past weekend, Sidwell Friends, which rejoined the Mid-Atlantic Conference this season, forfeited its league opener at St. James on Saturday, citing not enough healthy players.
Meanwhile, Central Maryland Christian, down to 18 players, has reduced its regular-season schedule to four games.
While the reasons are varied, the result is the same: fewer opportunities for players to compete and an increasingly unpredictable high school football schedule.
texts.5:
## **Crofton Remains Unbeaten**
Crofton was featured early this season after what was then considered an upset victory over Old Mill.
Now, the Wildcats have established themselves as the team to beat in Anne Arundel County. Crofton is the county’s lone 5-0 team and one of just 21 undefeated teams remaining in the MPSSAA.
Dominic Jackson delivered the latest heroics, scoring on a 3-yard run to lift Crofton to a 20-17 overtime victory over Chesapeake-AA.
The teams tied at 14 after regulation. Gary Windsor gave Chesapeake-AA a 17-14 lead in the first overtime with a 27-yard field goal, but Crofton answered with a touchdown to complete the comeback and remain unbeaten.
texts.6:
## **Got Your Number**
Northwestern-PG edged Bladensburg, 22-20, over the weekend, marking the third consecutive year the Wildcats have beaten the Mustangs.
While the streak is notable, it is even more remarkable that Bladensburg is the only team Northwestern-PG has beaten since 2019.
Since midseason 2019, Northwestern-PG is 4-2 against Bladensburg but 0-53 against all other opponents. The Wildcats’ last victory over anyone other than Bladensburg came on Oct. 12, 2019, when Northwestern-PG thrashed DuVal, 47-6.

**Edwin Washington Edwards** (August 7, 1927 – July 12, 2021)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-3) was an American politician who served as the 50th governor of Louisiana for four terms (1972–1980, 1984–1988, and 1992–1996). A member of the Democratic Party, he previously served as a U.S. representative for [Louisiana's 7th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana's_7th_congressional_district "Louisiana's 7th congressional district") from 1965 to 1972. He served twice as many elected terms as any other Louisiana chief executive. He served a total of almost 16 years in gubernatorial office, which at 5,784 days is the sixth-longest such tenure in post-Constitutional U.S. history.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-4)

An influential figure in Louisiana politics, Edwards, who was dubbed the "very last of the line of New DealSouthern Democrats",[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-laststand-5) was long dogged by charges of corruption. In 2001, he was found guilty of racketeering charges and sentenced to 10 years in federal prison. Edwards began serving his sentence in October 2002 in Fort Worth, Texas, and was later transferred to the federal facility in Oakdale, Louisiana. He was released from federal prison in January 2011, having served eight years.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-autogenerated2-6) He was also considered to be the last remnant of the political machine founded and led by Huey Long and Earl Long to serve as governor.
In 2014, Edwards again sought election to the U.S. House of Representatives, running to represent [Louisiana's 6th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana's_6th_congressional_district "Louisiana's 6th congressional district").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-congress2014-7) He placed first in the jungle primary, but was defeated by Republican Garret Graves by nearly 25 percentage points in the runoff election,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-8) assumed to be a sign of Edwards' precipitous decline in popularity due to his felony conviction, as well as the Republican Party of Louisiana's growing dominance over state politics.

## Early life and career
[edit]
Edwin Washington Edwards was born in rural Avoyelles Parish near Marksville on August 7, 1927.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-NYTObit-9) His father, Clarence Edwards, was a half-French CreolePresbyteriansharecropper, while his mother, the former Agnès Brouillette, was a French-speaking Catholic.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-10) Edwards' ancestors were among early Louisiana colonists from France who eventually settled in Avoyelles Parish, referred to as the original French Creoles.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-11) Like many 20th century politicians from Avoyelles, Edwards assumed that he had Cajun ancestry, when in fact he may have had none. His father was descended from a family in Kentucky that came to Louisiana during the American Civil War. His great-great-grandfather, William Edwards, was killed in Marksville at the beginning of the Civil War because of his pro-Union sentiment.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-William_Edwards-12)
The young Edwards had planned on a career as a preacher. As a young man, he did some preaching for the Marksville Church of the Nazarene. He served briefly in the U.S. Navy Air Corps near the end of World War II. After his return from the military, he graduated at the age of twenty-one from Louisiana State University Law Center and began practicing law in Crowley, the seat of Acadia Parish. He relocated there in 1949 after his sister, Audrey E. Isbell, who had moved there with her husband, told him there were few French-speaking attorneys in the southwestern Louisiana community._[citation needed_]

## Early life and career
Edwards entered politics through election to the Crowley City Council in 1954.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-returnguv-13) He was a member of the Democratic Party which, in that era, had a monopoly on public offices in Louisiana, but which fell out of favor in the late 20th century. Edwards remained on the Crowley council until his election to the Louisiana State Senate in 1964; in that race he defeated, in a major political upset in the Democratic primary, the incumbent Bill Cleveland, a Crowley businessman who had served for twenty years in both houses of the Louisiana legislature. Years later as governor, Edwards appointed Cleveland's daughter, Willie Mae Fulkerson (1924–2009), a former member of the Crowley City Council, to the Louisiana Board of Prisons.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-14)

## 1971–1972 campaign for governor
[edit]
Edwards as Congressman, circa 1969
In the election of 1971–1972, Edwards won the governorship after finishing first in a field of seventeen candidates in the Democratic primary, including the final race of former governor Jimmie Davis and Gillis Long, a relative of Huey Long. His greatest support came from southern Louisiana, particularly among its large numbers of Cajun, Creole, and African-American voters._[citation needed_]
Both Edwards and Johnston ran on reform-oriented platforms during the primary, but Edwards was more adept at making political deals and building alliances for the runoff round of voting. Edwards said that the major philosophical difference that he held with Johnston was in regard to their "awareness of problems of the poor".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-15) Johnston won the endorsement of Edwards' legislative colleague, Joe D. Waggonner of Bossier Parish, but the Shreveport state senator declined to accept Edwards' offer of a televised debate between the two.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-16)
Bill Dodd, who was defeated for state superintendent of education in the same election cycle that Edwards was winning the governorship in for the first time, attributed the Edwards victory in part to political kingmaker Louis J. Roussel Jr., of New Orleans. According to Dodd, Roussel "can do more than any other individual in Louisiana to elect any candidate he supports for any office in this state.... He is such a good administrator and motivator that he can put together an organization that will win in business and in politics."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-17)

## First two terms as governor, 1972–1980
[edit]
Edwards during his first term as governor.
Edwards with President Richard Nixon in 1972
Both in his political rhetoric and in his public persona, Edwards cast himself as a Louisiana populist in the tradition of Huey P. Long and Earl K. Long.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-laststand-5) He was inaugurated as governor on May 9, 1972. One of his first acts was to call for a constitutional convention to overhaul Louisiana's bulky charter._[citation needed_]
On taking office, Edwards hired J. Kelly Nix as his executive assistant and in 1974 elevated him to first executive assistant. In the second term, however, Nix left the administration to take office as the Louisiana state school superintendent.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-18) Dale Thorn, who had been Edwards' press secretary while he was in Congress, continued in that position for the first and most of the second Edwards terms. He was later associate commissioner of higher education for the Louisiana Board of Regents, and a journalism professor at Louisiana State University.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-19)

## First two terms as governor, 1972–1980
Under Edwards, [Michael H. O'Keefe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_O'Keefe_(Louisiana_politician) "Michael O'Keefe (Louisiana politician)") of New Orleans in 1976 was named president of the state Senate, an office that was held by the lieutenant governor prior to the implementation of the state Constitution of 1974. In 1983, as Edwards prepared to return to office, O'Keefe was engulfed in scandal and forced to resign as senate president. e was replaced by Edwards loyalist [Samuel B. Nunez Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_B._Nunez_Jr. "Samuel B. Nunez Jr."), of Chalmette in St. Bernard Parish. On the same day Edwards won election to a third term, O'Keefe lost his bid for a seventh term by a wide margin to state Rep. Ben Bagert. In 2013, O'Keefe was still serving time in prison for a 1999 conviction.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-20)
During his first two terms in office, Edwards developed a reputation for being a flamboyant politician. Charismatic, well dressed, and quick with clever one-liners and retorts, he maintained wide popularity._[citation needed_]

## 2014 Congressional election
As expected, Edwards as the principal Democratic candidate led the 2014 primary field for Congress with 77,862 votes (30.1 percent), winning every parish in the district.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-84) He then faced the Republican runner-up, Garret Graves, in the December 6 runoff election. Graves had received 70,706 "jungle primary" votes (27.4 percent). Losing Republican candidates were Paul Dietzel II, with 35,013 votes (13.6 percent), state Senator Dan Claitor with 26,520 (10.3 percent), and state Representative Lenar Whitney with 19,146 votes (7.4 percent).[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-85) Edwards lost to Graves by a 62–38 percent margin in the runoff. It was only the second loss of his political career.
However, in 2024, the election data analysis website Split Ticket found that Edwards had overperformed the Democratic baseline in the district with a Wins above replacement (WAR) score of D+24.5.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-:0-86)

## Edwards' record of longevity
[edit]
Edwards has the seventh longest gubernatorial tenure in post-Constitutional U.S. history at 5,784 days.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-Ostermeier-87) Few governors have served four four-year terms. Edwards followed George Wallace of Alabama, Jim Hunt of North Carolina, Bill Janklow of South Dakota, Terry Branstad of Iowa, Lewis Cass of Michigan, and Jim Rhodes of Ohio as 16-year governors. However, Branstad was elected to a fifth nonconsecutive term as governor of Iowa in 2010, placing him second to George Clinton of New York (21 years) as the longest-serving governor in U.S. history, and won a sixth term as governor in 2014.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-88) In December 2015 Branstad surpassed New York's George Clinton as the longest-tenured governor in American history, with 8,169 days in office.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-89)
Veteran journalist Iris Kelso once described Edwards as clearly "the most interesting" of the six governors that she had covered while working for three newspapers and WDSU, the NBC television affiliate in New Orleans. Kelso declared Edwards more colorful than Earl Long, whom she covered for less than a year in the office.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-90)

## Edwards' record of longevity
### Marriages and family
[edit]
In 1949, Edwards married Elaine Schwartzenburg, whom he had met at Marksville High School. The couple had four children, daughters Anna and Victoria and sons Stephen and David. In August 1972, Edwards appointed her as an interim U.S. senator to complete the unfinished term of Allen J. Ellender of Houma, who died while campaigning for his seventh term in office. Ellender was President pro tempore and chairman of the Committee on Appropriations at the time of his death. Elaine Edwards resigned seat six days after the election of Ellender's permanent successor, J. Bennett Johnston, in order to give Johnston seniority over other new senators elected on November 7, 1972 (including future PresidentJoe Biden).
On July 1, 1989, the couple divorced after forty years of marriage. They had begun living apart on March 15, 1988, the day after Edwards' third term ended. Mrs. Edwards did not reside at the [Louisiana Governor's Mansion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_Governor's_Mansion "Louisiana Governor's Mansion") during Edwin's third term, instead staying at the family's ranch in southeast Baton Rouge.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-91)
In 1994, Edwards married Candy Picou (born 1964). In 1997, the couple entered the headlines when they attempted to have a child. Edwards had a vasectomy reversal, and the couple froze sperm to attempt to have a baby but were not successful.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-returnguv-13)

## Edwards' record of longevity
### Marriages and family
In July 2011, Edwards married Trina Grimes, his prison pen pal. They began corresponding while he was serving his sentence for corruption. At the time of the wedding, he was 83, and she was 32.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-92) On August 1, 2013, Grimes gave birth to their child.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-93) In 2013, Edwards and Trina co-starred in an A&E reality show, _[The Governor's Wife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Governor's\_Wife "The Governor's Wife")_ based on their life together.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-kondolojy1-94)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-stanley1-95)
One of Edwards's brothers, Nolan Edwards, a former assistant district attorney in Acadia Parish, was murdered in Crowley by an irate client in 1983, the same year that Edwards was engineering his comeback bid for a third term as governor. Nolan's killer, Rodney Wingate Jr., of Church Point, Louisiana, then killed himself. Wingate had been pardoned by Governor Edwards in 1980 for two drug convictions in the 1970s, a pardon procured through the intervention of Nolan Edwards.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-96) Nolan's murder halted the 1983 politicking. Newspapers carried a photograph of brothers Edwin and Marion locked in an embrace on an airport tarmac.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-marion-35)

## Edwards' record of longevity
### Marriages and family
Marion Edwards, an insurance agent and political consultant, was a cancer survivor and counseled other patients for many years. Born on July 10, 1928, in Marksville, he died on January 12, 2013, at the age of eighty-four at his home in Broussard near Lafayette, Louisiana. The cause of death was not released. The Marion D. Edwards Fellowship in HepaticOncology at the M.D. Anderson Hospital and Tumor Institute in Houston, Texas, is named in his honor. Marion Edwards, who was Nazarene, was survived by his second wife, the former Deborah "Penny" Meaux, and three daughters from his first marriage to Aline Luther Edwards: Wanda Edwards, Elizabeth Kersten, and Donna Edwards.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-marde-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-marion-35)
Another brother, Allen Edwards, the longtime owner of a farm and heavy equipment company in Quitman in northern Arkansas, died in 2009, while Edwards was in prison. Edwards did not attend the funeral because of security difficulties.
Edwards was an uncle by marriage to former U.S. Representative Charles Boustany, a Republican from Lafayette, whose district includes much of the territory represented from 1965 to 1972 by then-U.S. Representative Edwin Edwards. Boustany's wife is the former Bridget Edwards, a daughter of Nolan Edwards.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-97)

# Edwards Haverhill Facility
## Our Facility
At Product Company Haverhill, we play a critical role in the Edwards global R&D and production capability for customers in the semiconductor market. Opened in 2023, our state-of-the-art 136,000 square foot facility in Massachusetts is home to R&D, manufacturing and warehousing for our cryogenic pump and chiller business.
Our team is working on some exciting technologies, innovative ways to increase production capacity, and effective cost-saving measures to better the environment. We hope to provide solutions and inspiration for other facilities, with an open invitation to partner with other Edwards and Atlas Copco entities in developing new technologies for the future.

# Edwards Haverhill Facility
## Our Products
The products produced by Edwards Haverhill are crucial to the manufacturing of the expanding global semiconductor industry and leading engineering markets.
**CTI-Cryogenic Pumps & Compressors**: From our single cryopumps used in a spectrum of high technology research applications to our sophisticated cryopump systems used in the manufacturing of semiconductor, flat panel, and optical devices, CTI-Cryogenics sets the standard for cryogenic high-vacuum technology.
**Polycold Chillers**: Polycold cryochillers are closed loop cryogenic refrigeration systems that provide up to 4,000 watts of cooling power with temperatures as low as -200 C. They can be used to condense water vapor within a vacuum process to significantly improve pump down time and vacuum quality. Polycold products can also be used in direct cooling applications like cooling electro-static chucks used in semi-conductor production or cooling various sensor technologies for improved signal capture.

## Our Women in Engineering
We are lucky to have many talented engineers at PC Haverhill, including four female engineers who were chosen to be featured as part of Atlas Copco’s female engineering program.
A film crew came to the facility to shoot videos of all four in their daily job roles as engineers.These videos were part of a marketing initiative called “Women in Engineering” where they met with 7 leading female engineers from across North America, to learn more about them, and their journeys.
The four women featured from Edwards Haverhill are: Lead Mechanical Engineer-Sustaining Ita Kane; Cryogenics Technologist Lydia Shen; Cryogenics Technologist Homa Ghasemi; and Mechanical Engineer Alana Guilbault. The videos were featured at the Society of Women Engineers Show in Chicago, and can be seen on Atlas Copco’s YouTube page.

# Edwards Haverhill Facility
## A Golden Achievement
Atlas Copco built the PC Haverhill facility with sustainability in mind.
It’s with that level of commitment and care for our planet that we are very proud to share some exciting news. Edwards Vacuum (PC Haverhill) has officially achieved its LEED Gold Certification following acceptance of the Design and Construction Final Review.
LEED Gold certification represents a significant achievement in sustainable building practices, and indicates that a building has met stringent sustainability criteria and demonstrates a commitment to environmental stewardship.

# Edwards Haverhill Facility
## Cryo Crew Softball is a Hit
Sharing quality time outside the office with fellow employees and being a part of the Haverhill community is what this team is all about. Improving the culture and bringing the facility together through wellbeing and inclusion.
The Cryo Crew is the only softball team in Haverill's Recreation League made up entirely of employees from the same company. In doing so, the team embraced their diversity and welcomed inclusion. They actually found strength in their differences, and celebrated the small victories of the team..
Even when the loses piled up, the teams attitude became stronger, and the team grew stronger. It wasnt about winning, it was about the comradely, the team building, the inclusion and diversity, and most of all, the fun of playing a simple game with your colleagues and enjoying their company.This simple mindset has made the Cryo Crew stronger and resilient. It has kick-started something that you can feel in the culture at Edwards PC Haverhill, and this is just the beginning.

## Early life and career
[edit]
Edwin Washington Edwards was born in rural Avoyelles Parish near Marksville on August 7, 1927.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-NYTObit-9) His father, Clarence Edwards, was a half-French CreolePresbyteriansharecropper, while his mother, the former Agnès Brouillette, was a French-speaking Catholic.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-10) Edwards' ancestors were among early Louisiana colonists from France who eventually settled in Avoyelles Parish, referred to as the original French Creoles.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-11) Like many 20th century politicians from Avoyelles, Edwards assumed that he had Cajun ancestry, when in fact he may have had none. His father was descended from a family in Kentucky that came to Louisiana during the American Civil War. His great-great-grandfather, William Edwards, was killed in Marksville at the beginning of the Civil War because of his pro-Union sentiment.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-William_Edwards-12)
The young Edwards had planned on a career as a preacher. As a young man, he did some preaching for the Marksville Church of the Nazarene. He served briefly in the U.S. Navy Air Corps near the end of World War II. After his return from the military, he graduated at the age of twenty-one from Louisiana State University Law Center and began practicing law in Crowley, the seat of Acadia Parish. He relocated there in 1949 after his sister, Audrey E. Isbell, who had moved there with her husband, told him there were few French-speaking attorneys in the southwestern Louisiana community._[citation needed_]
texts.5:
## Early life and career
Edwards entered politics through election to the Crowley City Council in 1954.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-returnguv-13) He was a member of the Democratic Party which, in that era, had a monopoly on public offices in Louisiana, but which fell out of favor in the late 20th century. Edwards remained on the Crowley council until his election to the Louisiana State Senate in 1964; in that race he defeated, in a major political upset in the Democratic primary, the incumbent Bill Cleveland, a Crowley businessman who had served for twenty years in both houses of the Louisiana legislature. Years later as governor, Edwards appointed Cleveland's daughter, Willie Mae Fulkerson (1924–2009), a former member of the Crowley City Council, to the Louisiana Board of Prisons.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-14)
texts.6:
## 1971–1972 campaign for governor
[edit]
Edwards as Congressman, circa 1969
In the election of 1971–1972, Edwards won the governorship after finishing first in a field of seventeen candidates in the Democratic primary, including the final race of former governor Jimmie Davis and Gillis Long, a relative of Huey Long. His greatest support came from southern Louisiana, particularly among its large numbers of Cajun, Creole, and African-American voters._[citation needed_]
Both Edwards and Johnston ran on reform-oriented platforms during the primary, but Edwards was more adept at making political deals and building alliances for the runoff round of voting. Edwards said that the major philosophical difference that he held with Johnston was in regard to their "awareness of problems of the poor".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-15) Johnston won the endorsement of Edwards' legislative colleague, Joe D. Waggonner of Bossier Parish, but the Shreveport state senator declined to accept Edwards' offer of a televised debate between the two.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-16)
Bill Dodd, who was defeated for state superintendent of education in the same election cycle that Edwards was winning the governorship in for the first time, attributed the Edwards victory in part to political kingmaker Louis J. Roussel Jr., of New Orleans. According to Dodd, Roussel "can do more than any other individual in Louisiana to elect any candidate he supports for any office in this state.... He is such a good administrator and motivator that he can put together an organization that will win in business and in politics."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-17)
texts.7:
## First two terms as governor, 1972–1980
[edit]
Edwards during his first term as governor.
Edwards with President Richard Nixon in 1972
Both in his political rhetoric and in his public persona, Edwards cast himself as a Louisiana populist in the tradition of Huey P. Long and Earl K. Long.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-laststand-5) He was inaugurated as governor on May 9, 1972. One of his first acts was to call for a constitutional convention to overhaul Louisiana's bulky charter._[citation needed_]
On taking office, Edwards hired J. Kelly Nix as his executive assistant and in 1974 elevated him to first executive assistant. In the second term, however, Nix left the administration to take office as the Louisiana state school superintendent.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-18) Dale Thorn, who had been Edwards' press secretary while he was in Congress, continued in that position for the first and most of the second Edwards terms. He was later associate commissioner of higher education for the Louisiana Board of Regents, and a journalism professor at Louisiana State University.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-19)
texts.8:
## First two terms as governor, 1972–1980
Under Edwards, [Michael H. O'Keefe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_O'Keefe_(Louisiana_politician) "Michael O'Keefe (Louisiana politician)") of New Orleans in 1976 was named president of the state Senate, an office that was held by the lieutenant governor prior to the implementation of the state Constitution of 1974. In 1983, as Edwards prepared to return to office, O'Keefe was engulfed in scandal and forced to resign as senate president. e was replaced by Edwards loyalist [Samuel B. Nunez Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_B._Nunez_Jr. "Samuel B. Nunez Jr."), of Chalmette in St. Bernard Parish. On the same day Edwards won election to a third term, O'Keefe lost his bid for a seventh term by a wide margin to state Rep. Ben Bagert. In 2013, O'Keefe was still serving time in prison for a 1999 conviction.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-20)
During his first two terms in office, Edwards developed a reputation for being a flamboyant politician. Charismatic, well dressed, and quick with clever one-liners and retorts, he maintained wide popularity._[citation needed_]
texts.34:
## 2014 Congressional election
As expected, Edwards as the principal Democratic candidate led the 2014 primary field for Congress with 77,862 votes (30.1 percent), winning every parish in the district.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-84) He then faced the Republican runner-up, Garret Graves, in the December 6 runoff election. Graves had received 70,706 "jungle primary" votes (27.4 percent). Losing Republican candidates were Paul Dietzel II, with 35,013 votes (13.6 percent), state Senator Dan Claitor with 26,520 (10.3 percent), and state Representative Lenar Whitney with 19,146 votes (7.4 percent).[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-85) Edwards lost to Graves by a 62–38 percent margin in the runoff. It was only the second loss of his political career.
However, in 2024, the election data analysis website Split Ticket found that Edwards had overperformed the Democratic baseline in the district with a Wins above replacement (WAR) score of D+24.5.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-:0-86)
texts.35:
## Edwards' record of longevity
[edit]
Edwards has the seventh longest gubernatorial tenure in post-Constitutional U.S. history at 5,784 days.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-Ostermeier-87) Few governors have served four four-year terms. Edwards followed George Wallace of Alabama, Jim Hunt of North Carolina, Bill Janklow of South Dakota, Terry Branstad of Iowa, Lewis Cass of Michigan, and Jim Rhodes of Ohio as 16-year governors. However, Branstad was elected to a fifth nonconsecutive term as governor of Iowa in 2010, placing him second to George Clinton of New York (21 years) as the longest-serving governor in U.S. history, and won a sixth term as governor in 2014.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-88) In December 2015 Branstad surpassed New York's George Clinton as the longest-tenured governor in American history, with 8,169 days in office.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-89)
Veteran journalist Iris Kelso once described Edwards as clearly "the most interesting" of the six governors that she had covered while working for three newspapers and WDSU, the NBC television affiliate in New Orleans. Kelso declared Edwards more colorful than Earl Long, whom she covered for less than a year in the office.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-90)
texts.36:
## Edwards' record of longevity
### Marriages and family
[edit]
In 1949, Edwards married Elaine Schwartzenburg, whom he had met at Marksville High School. The couple had four children, daughters Anna and Victoria and sons Stephen and David. In August 1972, Edwards appointed her as an interim U.S. senator to complete the unfinished term of Allen J. Ellender of Houma, who died while campaigning for his seventh term in office. Ellender was President pro tempore and chairman of the Committee on Appropriations at the time of his death. Elaine Edwards resigned seat six days after the election of Ellender's permanent successor, J. Bennett Johnston, in order to give Johnston seniority over other new senators elected on November 7, 1972 (including future PresidentJoe Biden).
On July 1, 1989, the couple divorced after forty years of marriage. They had begun living apart on March 15, 1988, the day after Edwards' third term ended. Mrs. Edwards did not reside at the [Louisiana Governor's Mansion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_Governor's_Mansion "Louisiana Governor's Mansion") during Edwin's third term, instead staying at the family's ranch in southeast Baton Rouge.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-91)
In 1994, Edwards married Candy Picou (born 1964). In 1997, the couple entered the headlines when they attempted to have a child. Edwards had a vasectomy reversal, and the couple froze sperm to attempt to have a baby but were not successful.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-returnguv-13)
texts.37:
## Edwards' record of longevity
### Marriages and family
In July 2011, Edwards married Trina Grimes, his prison pen pal. They began corresponding while he was serving his sentence for corruption. At the time of the wedding, he was 83, and she was 32.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-92) On August 1, 2013, Grimes gave birth to their child.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-93) In 2013, Edwards and Trina co-starred in an A&E reality show, _[The Governor's Wife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Governor's\_Wife "The Governor's Wife")_ based on their life together.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-kondolojy1-94)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-stanley1-95)
One of Edwards's brothers, Nolan Edwards, a former assistant district attorney in Acadia Parish, was murdered in Crowley by an irate client in 1983, the same year that Edwards was engineering his comeback bid for a third term as governor. Nolan's killer, Rodney Wingate Jr., of Church Point, Louisiana, then killed himself. Wingate had been pardoned by Governor Edwards in 1980 for two drug convictions in the 1970s, a pardon procured through the intervention of Nolan Edwards.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-96) Nolan's murder halted the 1983 politicking. Newspapers carried a photograph of brothers Edwin and Marion locked in an embrace on an airport tarmac.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-marion-35)
texts.38:
## Edwards' record of longevity
### Marriages and family
Marion Edwards, an insurance agent and political consultant, was a cancer survivor and counseled other patients for many years. Born on July 10, 1928, in Marksville, he died on January 12, 2013, at the age of eighty-four at his home in Broussard near Lafayette, Louisiana. The cause of death was not released. The Marion D. Edwards Fellowship in HepaticOncology at the M.D. Anderson Hospital and Tumor Institute in Houston, Texas, is named in his honor. Marion Edwards, who was Nazarene, was survived by his second wife, the former Deborah "Penny" Meaux, and three daughters from his first marriage to Aline Luther Edwards: Wanda Edwards, Elizabeth Kersten, and Donna Edwards.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-marde-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-marion-35)
Another brother, Allen Edwards, the longtime owner of a farm and heavy equipment company in Quitman in northern Arkansas, died in 2009, while Edwards was in prison. Edwards did not attend the funeral because of security difficulties.
Edwards was an uncle by marriage to former U.S. Representative Charles Boustany, a Republican from Lafayette, whose district includes much of the territory represented from 1965 to 1972 by then-U.S. Representative Edwin Edwards. Boustany's wife is the former Bridget Edwards, a daughter of Nolan Edwards.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Edwards#cite_note-97)

# Edwards Haverhill Facility
## Our Facility
At Product Company Haverhill, we play a critical role in the Edwards global R&D and production capability for customers in the semiconductor market. Opened in 2023, our state-of-the-art 136,000 square foot facility in Massachusetts is home to R&D, manufacturing and warehousing for our cryogenic pump and chiller business.
Our team is working on some exciting technologies, innovative ways to increase production capacity, and effective cost-saving measures to better the environment. We hope to provide solutions and inspiration for other facilities, with an open invitation to partner with other Edwards and Atlas Copco entities in developing new technologies for the future.
texts.7:
# Edwards Haverhill Facility
## Our Products
The products produced by Edwards Haverhill are crucial to the manufacturing of the expanding global semiconductor industry and leading engineering markets.
**CTI-Cryogenic Pumps & Compressors**: From our single cryopumps used in a spectrum of high technology research applications to our sophisticated cryopump systems used in the manufacturing of semiconductor, flat panel, and optical devices, CTI-Cryogenics sets the standard for cryogenic high-vacuum technology.
**Polycold Chillers**: Polycold cryochillers are closed loop cryogenic refrigeration systems that provide up to 4,000 watts of cooling power with temperatures as low as -200 C. They can be used to condense water vapor within a vacuum process to significantly improve pump down time and vacuum quality. Polycold products can also be used in direct cooling applications like cooling electro-static chucks used in semi-conductor production or cooling various sensor technologies for improved signal capture.

# Edwards Haverhill Facility
## Cryo Crew Softball is a Hit
Sharing quality time outside the office with fellow employees and being a part of the Haverhill community is what this team is all about. Improving the culture and bringing the facility together through wellbeing and inclusion.
The Cryo Crew is the only softball team in Haverill's Recreation League made up entirely of employees from the same company. In doing so, the team embraced their diversity and welcomed inclusion. They actually found strength in their differences, and celebrated the small victories of the team..
Even when the loses piled up, the teams attitude became stronger, and the team grew stronger. It wasnt about winning, it was about the comradely, the team building, the inclusion and diversity, and most of all, the fun of playing a simple game with your colleagues and enjoying their company.This simple mindset has made the Cryo Crew stronger and resilient. It has kick-started something that you can feel in the culture at Edwards PC Haverhill, and this is just the beginning.

Title: Fort Hill seeks 23rd straight win over Allegany
Chunks: 0,1,2
CUMBERLAND — Even after putting up a combined 91 points in the last two weeks, all wasn't perfect for Fort Hill.
Between the Sentinels' two games in Washington County, they committed more than 40 penalties.
Advertisement
Fort Hill has a chance to start fresh when it returns to Greenway Avenue Stadium for the annual Homecoming game against city rival Allegany on Saturday at 12:30 p.m.
The Sentinels, who wrapped up the top seed in the Class 1A West Region playoffs with last week's 49-14 thrashing over Smithsburg, haven't played at Greenway since Oct. 2.
Since their come-from-behind, 43-42 win over West Virginia power Bridgeport, the Sentinels have played at Mountain Ridge, North Hagerstown and Smithsburg.
Senior running back/linebacker Carson Bender admitted that the Sentinels had played a bit out of their element the past two weeks and a return to Greenway for Homecoming will be welcomed.
Advertisement
"It's definitely mental stuff," Bender said after the win over Smithsburg. "We gotta be able to keep our cool. You know, Washington County being there for two weeks now, obviously the penalties ramped up there.
"We gotta clean it up. I think being back at home and being in our element next week and throughout the playoffs, that'll help us out a lot."
No. 1 Fort Hill (8-0) and No. 4 Allegany (5-3) will meet for the 106th time. The Sentinels have won 22 straight over the Campers and lead the all-time series 69-32-4.
Fort Hill won last year's game 57-13, setting records for the largest margin of victory and most points in series history.
Advertisement
Braelyn Younger also rushed for a record 203 yards and equalled the all-time touchdown mark with five scores.
"They're playing each other sometimes since five or six years old up through the Pop Warner stages and JV levels," Fort Hill coach Zack Alkire said. "There's lots of familiarity between the kids and what each team can do.

"Both sides look forward to it, both players and coaches, and this year's no different. It's obviously one of the games we circle on the calendar. The kids are pretty amped up for it."
Sophomore Levi House will make his third consecutive start at quarterback in place of Brady O'Neal.
Advertisement
House moved over to signal-caller from the tight end spot starting with the North Hagerstown game. In that game, House threw just one incompletion as the Sentinels ran for 369 yards.
But in last week's matchup with Smithsburg, the Sentinels weren't able to pop off as many explosive runs, forcing House to resort to his arm more often.
House gave the Leopards' defense fits all night, completing 7 of 10 passes for 110 yards while adding 60 yards with his feet.
"He completed a lot of those passes," Alkire said. "He made a lot of good decisions. He made a couple other decisions to run the ball instead of throwing the ball. So (we're) really happy with Levi's progress at the quarterback position and look forward to seeing how he can open things up a little bit on Saturday."
Advertisement
The Sentinels still grounded 269 yards on the Leopards. Fort Hill's longest run was a 45-yard touchdown by Channing Logsdon in the first quarter. Its second-biggest run was a 20-yarder by House.
Ground yards won't be easy to come by against an Allegany team that's given up an average of 15.2 points during its five-game win streak.
Bender leads the Sentinels with 879 yards rushing and has 13 touchdowns. He also led the team with 96 yards last week.
Neek Taylor has contributed 730 yards and 15 touchdowns. Logsdon (345 yards) and Isaiah Welsh (262 yards) have also been vital parts of Fort Hill's ground game.
Advertisement
Defensively, Fort Hill has allowed just 98 points overall for an average of 12.3 per game.

"We gotta come off the football first and foremost," Alkire said. "Our offensive line needs to be able to track people off the ball without holding and blocking in the back. We need to cut down on the penalties from the previous two weeks and hold onto the football.
"We're gonna have to play really aggressive defense. We're gonna have to defend the pass when needed to, get pressure on the quarterback, make sure all of our gaps are filled and be aggressive running towards the football."
Since there are only seven teams in the West Region, Fort Hill will receive a first-round bye.
Advertisement
As it stands now, Allegany is the No. 4 seed and will meet No. 5 Southern in the quarterfinals.
A Campers win in that game would set up a rematch between the city rivals in the region semifinals.
Fort Hill and Allegany played once last season, but met twice in 2024. The Sentinels won both games by an 87-0 margin on their way to an 11th state title.
"Homecoming's an important game for the community for both sides," Alkire said. "It's a game that you obviously wanna win. But the reality of it is that the playoffs are coming and a win would really give you a lot of momentum going into the playoffs."

Source: https://www.cnhi.com/rss_feed/fort-hill-dunbar-through-the-years/
Title: Fort Hill-Dunbar, through the years - CNHI
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
September 11, 2024 by
Rivalries come in all shapes and sizes.
Some are marked by their frequency and tradition — think Fort Hill-Allegany or Allegany-Keyser, both spanning more than 100 games. Others, like the Steelers-Raiders in the ‘70s and Patriots-Colts during the 2000s, blossomed due to recurrent high-stakes matchups.
Fort Hill and Dunbar fit into that second group. All six of their meetings have come with championships on the line: five in state title games and once in a semifinal.
That will change at Morgan State on Friday. For the first time in history, Fort Hill and Dunbar, holders of a combined 23 championships between them, link up in the regular season.
Due to reclassification, the teams won’t play for a title any time soon.
Since the state moved to a six class system in 2021, Dunbar and Fort Hill have won all three state titles in Class 2A/1A and 1A, respectively.
That doesn’t mean Friday’s contest is without stakes. The winner will hold the longest win streak in the state of Maryland.
Dunbar already does, boasting 38 wins in a row, while Fort Hill is second with 22 consecutive triumphs.
The Poets also have their sights on the all-time Maryland record for consecutive victories of 53, set by Damascus from 2015-18, which they could achieve next season.
Furthermore, there is intrigue surrounding the timing of the matchup, as both are in position to tie a state record with a fourth consecutive state championship this year.
Fort Hill shares the current high mark with Urbana (1998-01), winning four in a row under Hall of Fame coach Todd Appel from 2013-16.
Before getting into the Dunbar-Fort Hill series, in which the Poets hold a 5-1 edge, it’s worth highlighting the last time a Cumberland school played, and beat, the Baltimore City power.
In Week 1 of 2017, Allegany welcomed Dunbar to Greenway Avenue Stadium and the two produced an all-time offensive classic that featured a combined 91 points, 43 first downs and 906 yards of offense.

Elisha Llewellyn and Karson Robinette accounted for nearly 500 yards between them, and Allegany sent the Poets back East packing with a 49-42 defeat.
The loss lit a fire in Dunbar, whose season ended with hardware earned from toppling the Campers’ crosstown rival, but more on that later.
We’ll begin our journey with Fort Hill’s lone victory in the series and then travel back in time chronologically.
1997
Fort Hill 22, Dunbar 6
Led by the rushing of hard-nosed fullback Josh Page, Fort Hill avenged its loss to the Poets three years prior to end a 22-year championship drought in College Park.
The 6-foot-3, 220-pound back pounded Dunbar to the tune of 125 yards and two touchdowns on 33 carries. He finished his career with then-state records in 71 touchdowns and 438 points and an area record 4,987 rushing yards.
Fort Hill finished with a 13-0 record punctuated by the Class 2A title.
The result is the most lopsided in series history. Dunbar has won by 15 twice, and the last three meetings have been decided by six points or less.
It was the lone championship for Hall of Fame coach Mike Calhoun, who guided Fort Hill to five title games and four in his final five years. He finished with a 122-31 record.
2017
Dunbar 30, Fort Hill 26
With Fort Hill aiming for a record fifth consecutive state championship, Dunbar scored the second-half’s lone touchdown, an 87-yard passing score in the third quarter, to deny the Sentinels in Annapolis.
Fort Hill (12-2) led 26-22 at halftime, but Dunbar adjusted to load the box and deny Troy Banks, who finished with 153 yards on 35 carries.
Dunbar (12-1) won the second half 8-0 and the game on Jared Lewis’ short pass to Ryan Wood that resulted in an 87-yard house call.

The clash of styles was evident by the teams’ scoring drives. Dunbar scored six points on a 68-yard run and passes for 60, 63 and 87 yards. Fort Hill on sustained 69-, 77- and 88-yard series.
Luke Hamilton, Carter Swan, Wyatt Brehm, Kaleb Harden and Braeden Smith led the Fort Hill defense.
The championship game appearance was the fifth of six in a row for Fort Hill under Hall of Fame coach Todd Appel, a state record. Appel finished with a 142-16 record and won five Class 1A state titles.
Appel is now the defensive coordinator at Stephen Decatur in Berlin, which he helped to a Class 2A state championship last year. It was the school’s first.
2010
Dunbar 20, Fort Hill 14
In the lone matchup that wasn’t for a state championship, little 5-foot-6, 140-pound Dunbar quarterback Kevin Estep snuck over the line with three seconds left at Baltimore Poly’s Lumsden Scott Stadium to advance to the title game.
The touchdown came on fourth-and-goal and broke a 14-all tie. Fort Hill drew even on a 30-yard pop pass from Dylan Clay to Justin Dawson with 5:20 left in the third quarter. Joe Howser found Dawson on the two-point conversion.
Garrett Clay finished with 118 yards on 16 carries to top Fort Hill (9-4).
“They pushed us around,” Dunbar coach Lawrence Smith recalled at the time. “They pushed us down the field. Our defense was sucking wind.”
Fort Hill gave a miraculous defensive effort to hold down a Dunbar (12-1) team led by workhorse back Epenetus Henriques, who had 33 carries for 224 yards.
Dunbar went on to score 22 unanswered points in the championship game to defeat Havre de Grace, 22-12, and lift the Class 1A title.
2008
Dunbar 20, Fort Hill 19
Dunbar’s Tavon Austin went down as one of, if not the greatest scholastic football player in state history, and Fort Hill was one stop short of doing the impossible.

The Poets (13-1) drove 91 yards in the final two minutes, and Austin went around the left side of his line for the winning two-point conversion. Jonathan Perry connected with Sean Farr for the touchdown at Baltimore’s M&T Bank Stadium.
Austin still holds career state records for total offense (9,258), rushing yards (7,962), points (790) and touchdowns (123). He rushed for 2,660 yards and 34 touchdowns on just 218 carries as a senior.
Against Fort Hill (11-2), he finished with 191 yards on 28 carries and scored a pair of touchdowns to clinch a three-peat against Cumberland city schools. Dunbar beat Fort Hill in the ‘06 title game and Allegany in ‘07.
Austin would go on to an All-American career at West Virginia and was selected eighth overall by the Rams. He played nine NFL seasons, officially retiring this August.
It was a heartbreaker for Fort Hill, which missed a 37-yard field goal with two minutes to go that would have iced the game.
The closeness of the game shocked coach Smith, whose Poets got all they could handle from the Sentinels in Appel’s first season.
Marcus Lashley scored two touchdowns for Fort Hill, and Eric Howser accounted for the other.
2006
Dunbar 38, Fort Hill 23
Dunbar racked up 549 yards of offense led by Austin and Marice Portee to turn back Barry Lattimer’s Fort Hill at Ravens Stadium.
The duo accounted for a combined 453 yards of offense. Fort Hill held Austin to just eight rushing yards on four carries in the first half, but Marice Portee exploded for 195 yards to keep the Poets afloat until Austin found his rhythm.
Austin rushed for 113 yards and three scores in the second half, and Portee led the way with 237 yards for the game.
Fort Hill (12-2) turned the ball over three times, and Dunbar (11-3) turned two of those into touchdowns.
Drew Yurko paced Fort Hill with 109 yards and a touchdown on 17 carries. Scott Rice added two scores.
1994

CUMBERLAND — Even after putting up a combined 91 points in the last two weeks, all wasn't perfect for Fort Hill.
Between the Sentinels' two games in Washington County, they committed more than 40 penalties.
Advertisement
Fort Hill has a chance to start fresh when it returns to Greenway Avenue Stadium for the annual Homecoming game against city rival Allegany on Saturday at 12:30 p.m.
The Sentinels, who wrapped up the top seed in the Class 1A West Region playoffs with last week's 49-14 thrashing over Smithsburg, haven't played at Greenway since Oct. 2.
Since their come-from-behind, 43-42 win over West Virginia power Bridgeport, the Sentinels have played at Mountain Ridge, North Hagerstown and Smithsburg.
Senior running back/linebacker Carson Bender admitted that the Sentinels had played a bit out of their element the past two weeks and a return to Greenway for Homecoming will be welcomed.
Advertisement
"It's definitely mental stuff," Bender said after the win over Smithsburg. "We gotta be able to keep our cool. You know, Washington County being there for two weeks now, obviously the penalties ramped up there.
"We gotta clean it up. I think being back at home and being in our element next week and throughout the playoffs, that'll help us out a lot."
No. 1 Fort Hill (8-0) and No. 4 Allegany (5-3) will meet for the 106th time. The Sentinels have won 22 straight over the Campers and lead the all-time series 69-32-4.
Fort Hill won last year's game 57-13, setting records for the largest margin of victory and most points in series history.
Advertisement
Braelyn Younger also rushed for a record 203 yards and equalled the all-time touchdown mark with five scores.
"They're playing each other sometimes since five or six years old up through the Pop Warner stages and JV levels," Fort Hill coach Zack Alkire said. "There's lots of familiarity between the kids and what each team can do.
texts.1:
"Both sides look forward to it, both players and coaches, and this year's no different. It's obviously one of the games we circle on the calendar. The kids are pretty amped up for it."
Sophomore Levi House will make his third consecutive start at quarterback in place of Brady O'Neal.
Advertisement
House moved over to signal-caller from the tight end spot starting with the North Hagerstown game. In that game, House threw just one incompletion as the Sentinels ran for 369 yards.
But in last week's matchup with Smithsburg, the Sentinels weren't able to pop off as many explosive runs, forcing House to resort to his arm more often.
House gave the Leopards' defense fits all night, completing 7 of 10 passes for 110 yards while adding 60 yards with his feet.
"He completed a lot of those passes," Alkire said. "He made a lot of good decisions. He made a couple other decisions to run the ball instead of throwing the ball. So (we're) really happy with Levi's progress at the quarterback position and look forward to seeing how he can open things up a little bit on Saturday."
Advertisement
The Sentinels still grounded 269 yards on the Leopards. Fort Hill's longest run was a 45-yard touchdown by Channing Logsdon in the first quarter. Its second-biggest run was a 20-yarder by House.
Ground yards won't be easy to come by against an Allegany team that's given up an average of 15.2 points during its five-game win streak.
Bender leads the Sentinels with 879 yards rushing and has 13 touchdowns. He also led the team with 96 yards last week.
Neek Taylor has contributed 730 yards and 15 touchdowns. Logsdon (345 yards) and Isaiah Welsh (262 yards) have also been vital parts of Fort Hill's ground game.
Advertisement
Defensively, Fort Hill has allowed just 98 points overall for an average of 12.3 per game.
texts.2:
"We gotta come off the football first and foremost," Alkire said. "Our offensive line needs to be able to track people off the ball without holding and blocking in the back. We need to cut down on the penalties from the previous two weeks and hold onto the football.
"We're gonna have to play really aggressive defense. We're gonna have to defend the pass when needed to, get pressure on the quarterback, make sure all of our gaps are filled and be aggressive running towards the football."
Since there are only seven teams in the West Region, Fort Hill will receive a first-round bye.
Advertisement
As it stands now, Allegany is the No. 4 seed and will meet No. 5 Southern in the quarterfinals.
A Campers win in that game would set up a rematch between the city rivals in the region semifinals.
Fort Hill and Allegany played once last season, but met twice in 2024. The Sentinels won both games by an 87-0 margin on their way to an 11th state title.
"Homecoming's an important game for the community for both sides," Alkire said. "It's a game that you obviously wanna win. But the reality of it is that the playoffs are coming and a win would really give you a lot of momentum going into the playoffs."

The championship game appearance was the fifth of six in a row for Fort Hill under Hall of Fame coach Todd Appel, a state record. Appel finished with a 142-16 record and won five Class 1A state titles.
Appel is now the defensive coordinator at Stephen Decatur in Berlin, which he helped to a Class 2A state championship last year. It was the school’s first.
2010
Dunbar 20, Fort Hill 14
In the lone matchup that wasn’t for a state championship, little 5-foot-6, 140-pound Dunbar quarterback Kevin Estep snuck over the line with three seconds left at Baltimore Poly’s Lumsden Scott Stadium to advance to the title game.
The touchdown came on fourth-and-goal and broke a 14-all tie. Fort Hill drew even on a 30-yard pop pass from Dylan Clay to Justin Dawson with 5:20 left in the third quarter. Joe Howser found Dawson on the two-point conversion.
Garrett Clay finished with 118 yards on 16 carries to top Fort Hill (9-4).
“They pushed us around,” Dunbar coach Lawrence Smith recalled at the time. “They pushed us down the field. Our defense was sucking wind.”
Fort Hill gave a miraculous defensive effort to hold down a Dunbar (12-1) team led by workhorse back Epenetus Henriques, who had 33 carries for 224 yards.
Dunbar went on to score 22 unanswered points in the championship game to defeat Havre de Grace, 22-12, and lift the Class 1A title.
2008
Dunbar 20, Fort Hill 19
Dunbar’s Tavon Austin went down as one of, if not the greatest scholastic football player in state history, and Fort Hill was one stop short of doing the impossible.
texts.3:
The Poets (13-1) drove 91 yards in the final two minutes, and Austin went around the left side of his line for the winning two-point conversion. Jonathan Perry connected with Sean Farr for the touchdown at Baltimore’s M&T Bank Stadium.
Austin still holds career state records for total offense (9,258), rushing yards (7,962), points (790) and touchdowns (123). He rushed for 2,660 yards and 34 touchdowns on just 218 carries as a senior.
Against Fort Hill (11-2), he finished with 191 yards on 28 carries and scored a pair of touchdowns to clinch a three-peat against Cumberland city schools. Dunbar beat Fort Hill in the ‘06 title game and Allegany in ‘07.
Austin would go on to an All-American career at West Virginia and was selected eighth overall by the Rams. He played nine NFL seasons, officially retiring this August.
It was a heartbreaker for Fort Hill, which missed a 37-yard field goal with two minutes to go that would have iced the game.
The closeness of the game shocked coach Smith, whose Poets got all they could handle from the Sentinels in Appel’s first season.
Marcus Lashley scored two touchdowns for Fort Hill, and Eric Howser accounted for the other.
2006
Dunbar 38, Fort Hill 23
Dunbar racked up 549 yards of offense led by Austin and Marice Portee to turn back Barry Lattimer’s Fort Hill at Ravens Stadium.
The duo accounted for a combined 453 yards of offense. Fort Hill held Austin to just eight rushing yards on four carries in the first half, but Marice Portee exploded for 195 yards to keep the Poets afloat until Austin found his rhythm.
Austin rushed for 113 yards and three scores in the second half, and Portee led the way with 237 yards for the game.
Fort Hill (12-2) turned the ball over three times, and Dunbar (11-3) turned two of those into touchdowns.
Drew Yurko paced Fort Hill with 109 yards and a touchdown on 17 carries. Scott Rice added two scores.
